questions.q: In `FROM c`, what does the alias `c` actually refer to?
options: A conventional stand-in for "every item in this container" — there's no table literally named c
A specific table named 'c' that must exist in the database
A shorthand for 'column', selecting all columns
The name of the Cosmos DB account
questions.explain: c is just a conventional alias, the same way SELECT * is a convention in relational SQL — it doesn't refer to a literal table.

questions.q: What does `SELECT VALUE c.name FROM c` do differently from `SELECT c.name FROM c`?
options: It returns bare values directly instead of wrapping each result in a JSON object
It deletes the name property from each document
It only works on numeric properties
It performs a cross-partition query while SELECT does not
questions.explain: SELECT VALUE strips the JSON wrapper, returning the raw scalar or array values instead of {"name": "..."} objects.

questions.q: A query uses `JOIN tag IN c.tags`. What is this JOIN actually doing?
options: Unwinding an array property inside a single document into multiple result rows — an intra-document join, not a join to another table
Joining the container to a second container named 'tags'
Performing a relational foreign-key join, identical to T-SQL
Filtering out documents that don't have a tags property
questions.explain: This JOIN never leaves the document — it unwinds an array property within that one document, closer to CROSS APPLY over JSON in T-SQL.

questions.q: Why would a relational DBA reach for `IS_DEFINED()` in a Cosmos DB query?
options: Because documents in the same container aren't validated against a fixed schema, so a property might not exist on every document
Because it checks whether a stored procedure is registered
Because it verifies the partition key is set correctly
Because it's required syntax on every WHERE clause
questions.explain: Without a schema to enforce shape, IS_DEFINED() lets a query safely check whether an optional property exists before referencing it.

questions.q: Why does filtering a query on the partition key make it cheaper than a query without that filter?
options: It can be routed directly to a single physical partition instead of being fanned out across every partition in the container
Partition key filters bypass request unit charges entirely
It converts the query into a stored procedure automatically
There is no real difference in cost — RU cost is fixed per query regardless of filters
questions.explain: A partition-key-filtered query targets one physical partition; without it, the query becomes a cross-partition fan-out that costs more RUs and latency.
